newsitem.title: UK: Long, dirty election campaign ahead for Britain.
newsitem.headline: Long, dirty election campaign ahead for Britain.

text.p: Britain's "pre-campaign tension" is finally over, but those hoping John Major's Conservatives and a resurgent Labour party will conduct an inspiring battle of ideas and ideals are likely to be disappointed.

If the events of the past two years are anything to go by, the election campaign will be remembered more for shadow-boxing and below-the-belt punches than for illuminating debate on which party is best suited to take Britain into the 21st century.

Negative campaigning and scare-mongering are sure to dominate the next six weeks after Prime Minister Major's announcement on Monday of a May 1 election. Voters could find the first head-to-head television debates in British politics one of the few illuminating moments in the longest campaign since 1918.

Britons are resigned to a dirty battle. In a January opinion poll, 74 percent of all voters said they expected a negative campaign from the Conservatives and 54 percent thought Labour would concentrate on attacking the government rather than setting out its alternative policies.

The Conservatives, harking back to their successful "Don't Trust Labour" campaign of 1992, will warn that, with the economy purring along nicely, now is not the time to take a risk on Labour with its past reputation for high taxes and overspending.

"The Tories (Conservatives) will fight the most negative campaign in the history of modern politics. They will tell lies about Labour. They will use the only weapon they have after running the most discredited government in modern times -- fear," Labour leader Tony Blair said recently.
Labour, sitting on a huge opinion poll lead, will point up the failings of 18 years of Conservative rule.
But Blair, warning that Labour cannot sit back and hope voters say "enough is enough", also relishes the chance to set out his stall and show how Labour could make a difference.
Major names this "time for a change" factor as his party's phantom enemy but believes his radical plans to shake up the welfare state will let him show he has not run out of ideas.
"If people are looking for change -- we are the change, and we'll carry forward what we've been doing for the last 18 years," he said on Monday as he announced the election.
Major has pledged to "smoke out" the inexperienced Blair and reveal Labour's true agenda, or lack of it, if it took power.

Labour will shy away from controversial subjects likely to frighten middle-class voters or expose splits between modernists and its old-style left wing. It will counter Conservative attacks with the line "same old Tories, same old lies".

"It is the politics of yawn and there is a real danger that Britain will go to sleep in the election and will sleepwalk into the next century," claims Liberal Democrat leader Paddy Ashdown. Labour's popularity is due largely to the moderate policies introduced by Blair since he was elected leader in July 1994, but these same policies could put a dampener on the campaign.
In several key policy areas there is now little difference between the positions of the two main parties.

In the past few months Labour's first reaction to a Conservative pledge has been to copy it, a move labelled "synchronised swimming" by Ashdown, whose party's support is being squeezed by Labour's move to the centre. Major says he will concentrate on the economy, ties with the European Union and the constitution as he believes voters prefer the Conservative position on these policies.
But the two parties' stances over Europe and the economy have been thoroughly debated over the past 12 months. The constitution raises little interest outside Scotland and Wales.

Labour has said it will reform the upper House of Lords and introduce a form of self-government for Scotland and Wales. It has also pledged to introduce a minimum wage and to adopt the Maastricht Treaty's Social Chapter on workers' rights.

But the party has cast off most of the socialist baggage that used to worry the middle classes, including a commitment to widespread nationalisation. Its traditional paymasters, the trade unions, have also been told to expect no favours.
Tax policy is not likely to dominate debate, as it did in 1992 when Conservative attacks on Labour tax plans scared voters in the final days of the campaign and let Major grab a shock victory.

Labour has promised to freeze income tax rates for five years. It has also drilled into voters' heads that, despite pledging not to raise taxes during the 1992 campaign, the Conservatives have introduced 22 tax rises in the past five years.
"The 1997 tax bombshell has been defused ... tax and spend is buried. Instead Labour will "save and invest"," Blair says, pointing to the health service and education as his priorities.

A live television debate between the two leaders is still uncertain because Ashdown is demanding to take part too. But if it does occur it will be fascinating to see how Major's ordinariness contrasts with Blair's more polished projection.
Labour plans to target the "grey man" of British politics, in particular Major's "weakness, drift and appeasement of the warring factions in his party".
Conservatives, however, believe Major is their trump card, his steady-as-you-go attitude to be preferred to Blair's flashiness.
